title: Mosquitoes are a choice - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Works in Progress argues that dengue, malaria and other mosquito-borne diseases are resurging in the US (dengue cases up 360% in 2024) but could be eliminated with engineered (Oxitec) or Wolbachia-infected (MosquitoMate, Google Debug) mosquitoes, which have proven 80-95% population reductions. The binding constraint is a 1986-era regulatory framework that bounced Oxitec between USDA, FDA and EPA for a decade; the author proposes FDA-style user fees and more reviewers to fix EPA throughput.

themes.theme: Resurgence of mosquito-borne disease in the US

insights.claim: The US reported almost 4,000 dengue cases in 2024, a 360% increase over the prior decade's average of 830 per year, with local transmission in Florida, California and Texas and Puerto Rico declaring a dengue public health emergency.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Dengue is no longer an imported-only disease in the US, raising demand for vector-control products and public-health spending in southern states.
insights.quote: In 2024, the country reported almost 4,000 cases of dengue, a 360 percent increase over the average of 830 per year over the previous decade

insights.claim: Ten locally acquired malaria cases were reported in the US in 2023, the first in twenty years; yellow fever remains absent but its mosquito vectors are still present.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Re-emergence of locally transmitted malaria signals that eliminated diseases can return as climate and vector conditions shift.

insights.claim: Rising temperatures and mosquito resistance to pesticides are driving the return of mosquito-borne diseases in the United States.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Pesticide resistance erodes the incumbent toolkit, creating an opening for biological and genetic vector-control alternatives.
insights.locator: Most Americans think of mosquito-borne diseases

insights.claim: The US is well-resourced enough and its disease-carrying mosquito population small enough that it could eliminate mosquito-borne diseases within its borders; the main obstacle is that the technology has spent fifteen years in regulatory limbo.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Frames the problem as regulatory rather than technical: policy reform, not R&D, is the binding constraint on market adoption.
insights.quote: The reason we haven’t is that the technology has spent fifteen years in regulatory limbo.
insights.locator: But we don’t have to accept this threat.

insights.claim: Oxitec's engineered male Aedes aegypti carry a tTAV lethal gene, suppressed in the lab by tetracycline, that kills female offspring in the wild while males pass it on for a few generations before it disappears, making it both multi-generational and self-limiting.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A self-limiting design reduces the need for continuous releases while limiting ecological persistence, a key argument for regulators and the public.
insights.locator: The scientists then formed a company, Oxitec

insights.claim: Sustained Oxitec releases cut wild Aedes aegypti populations by 80% in the Cayman Islands and by about 95% in a field trial in Juazeiro, Brazil.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Efficacy is demonstrated; commercialization risk sits in approvals, not performance.
insights.locator: Yet the technique is hugely effective.

insights.claim: Oxitec's US approval bounced between agencies: the USDA took 18 months to redirect it to the FDA, the FDA held it five years before carving out mosquito population control and passing it to the EPA, which granted only an Experimental Use Permit in May 2020, a decade after the 2010 submission.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Jurisdictional ambiguity alone can consume a decade, a major hidden cost and timeline risk for novel biotech ventures.

insights.claim: The FDA had claimed jurisdiction over genetically modified animals by treating altered genomic DNA as a veterinary drug, a category the author calls a poor fit for engineered mosquitoes.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Legacy legal categories map poorly onto new biotech, producing delays unrelated to safety.
insights.quote: ‘altered genomic DNA in an animal is a drug … because such altered DNA is an article intended to affect the structure or function of the body of the animal’

insights.claim: Oxitec's 2022 EPA expansion cleared up to 2.4 billion engineered mosquitoes across Florida and California, but releases were paused after public pushback; its permit expired in April 2024 and full registration remains pending, with a scientific advisory panel planned for November 2025 postponed indefinitely.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Public acceptance and regulatory scheduling remain open-ended risks for genetically engineered vector control in the US.

insights.claim: Local operators cite regulation as the main barrier: the Florida Keys Mosquito Control District's director said their biggest challenge has been awaiting regulatory approvals.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Demand from local mosquito districts exists; supply is gated by federal approval.
insights.quote: ‘our biggest challenges have been awaiting regulatory approvals.’
insights.locator: As Florida Keys Mosquito Control District

themes.theme: Sterile insect technique precedent and screwworm

insights.claim: The USDA has used radiation-based sterile insect technique since the 1950s, clearing screwworm from the US in the 1960s and pushing it back to Panama, saving American cattle farmers an estimated close to $800 million per year plus billions in wider economic benefits.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Mass insect release has a long record of large economic returns, supporting the case for analogous mosquito programs.

insights.claim: Containment of screwworm broke: in June 2026 Texas detected the first US case in 60 years, likely aided by cattle smuggling from Central America where the pest has resurged, and officials are redeploying sterile flies amid billions of dollars in damages.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Screwworm re-emergence is a live risk to US cattle supply and livestock economics.
insights.quote: in June 2026, Texas detected the United States’ first case of screwworm in 60 years, likely aided by cattle smuggling from Central America

insights.claim: Sterile fly releases have also suppressed the Mediterranean fruit fly in California and Florida; resettlement in California alone could cost over $1 billion per year in crop damage.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Agricultural pest control is a proven, high-value market for insect-release technologies.

insights.claim: Wolbachia, a bacterium naturally infecting roughly 60% of insect species, reduces mosquitoes' ability to carry viruses and causes eggs from infected males and uninfected females not to develop, enabling either population replacement or suppression without genetic modification.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Non-GM approach offers a less regulated path for vector control.

insights.claim: In a randomized trial in Singapore, releases of Wolbachia-infected male mosquitoes cut mosquito populations by 85% versus control areas and dengue infections by roughly 70%.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: City-scale evidence of disease reduction strengthens public-health procurement cases.
insights.locator: The approach has succeeded at the scale

insights.claim: In April 2024 MosquitoMate became the first company to receive full nationwide US commercial registration for a live mosquito biopesticide, after fifteen years in the system; Florida Keys (2025) and San Gabriel Valley (2026) districts quickly adopted it.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: First-mover registration gives MosquitoMate a regulatory moat while adoption by districts signals real demand.

insights.claim: Google's Debug project in June 2026 requested EPA approval to release 64 million Wolbachia mosquitoes targeting Culex quinquefasciatus (West Nile vector) in California and Florida, but must restart the Experimental Use Permit process despite using the same underlying technology.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Big-tech entry validates the market, but lack of precedent-reuse in approvals keeps time-to-market long even for well-funded entrants.
insights.locator: The technology is also attracting interest

insights.claim: No major new US biotech regulation has passed since the 1980s; the 1986 Coordinated Framework still divides jurisdiction using last-century categories, and agencies are not resourced or designed for speed.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Structural regulatory lag is a systemic headwind for US biotech commercialization across categories, not just mosquitoes.

insights.claim: Jurisdictional ambiguity also stalled cell-cultured meat between FDA and USDA until Congress forced a split review; a single early interagency meeting could have saved Oxitec years.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Early clarity on lead agency is a cheap fix with outsized time savings for novel products.

insights.claim: Biden's 2022 executive order directed agencies to resolve biotech regulatory uncertainty and update the Coordinated Framework, but almost none happened and Trump rescinded it in March 2025.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Policy reform momentum has stalled; investors should not assume near-term regulatory harmonization.

insights.claim: The EPA's 2022 Vector Expedited Review Voucher rewards novel mosquito-product registrants with faster review on their next application, but the author argues it does nothing about the backlog itself.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Voucher schemes favor incumbents with one approval already, while overall throughput stays constrained.

insights.claim: The EPA unit reviewing new mosquito control products is a small office handling everything from biochemicals to engineered mosquitoes, applying conventional pesticide protocols despite different questions of dispersal, inheritance and population impact.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Capacity and protocol mismatch at a single small office is a bottleneck for the entire biological vector-control sector.

insights.claim: Under the 1992 Prescription Drug User Fee Act, two thirds of the FDA's drug-review budget comes from industry fees; median review time fell from 29 months in the late 1980s to targets of ten months (standard) and six (priority), mostly met.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A proven funding template exists to accelerate approvals; extending it to the EPA would shorten biotech time-to-market.

insights.claim: Review times at the FDA fell by an estimated 3.3 months for every 100 reviewers added, whereas the EPA relies on Congress for two thirds of its budget and fees for only one third.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Staffing directly drives approval speed; EPA's appropriations dependence explains its slower throughput and points to fee reform as the lever.
insights.quote: review times fell by roughly 3.3 months for every 100 reviewers the FDA added

insights.claim: The author argues mosquito-borne disease is now a policy choice in the US: the tools to eliminate it exist and only regulatory will is lacking.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: If reform arrives, a substantial domestic market for engineered and Wolbachia mosquito products could open rapidly.
insights.quote: New technologies mean that mosquito-borne disease is now a choice in the United States.
insights.locator: It shouldn’t have to take fifteen years
